articles.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum cuts HPV levels by up to 93%
articles.summary: A specially engineered chewing gum reduced HPV by up to 93% and nearly eliminated two bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. The treatment preserved beneficial mouth bacteria, raising hopes for a safer and more affordable therapy.
articles.content:
Researchers have developed a bioengineered chewing gum that may offer a new way to target microbes associated with head and neck cancer. In tests involving oral samples from patients, extracts from the gum sharply reduced one virus and two types of bacteria linked to the disease.

The research team was led by Henry Daniell of the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The findings were published in Scientific Reports and could support the development of more accessible and affordable treatments.

A Need for Better Head and Neck Cancer Therapies

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that begins in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. The disease can be particularly aggressive, and outcomes are often poor when it is discovered at a later stage.

Daniell says that many recently approved cancer medications have not produced major improvements in patients' quality of life or five-year survival. That limited progress highlights the need for new approaches that can work alongside existing treatments.

Targeting HPV and Harmful Oral Bacteria

The new study builds on earlier research involving chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). The gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring antiviral protein.

Daniell and his colleagues used oral samples from patients with HNSCC to study three microbes associated with cancer. These included human papillomavirus, or HPV, along with two bacterial species, Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn).

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies."

Gum Extracts Sharply Reduce Microbe Levels

Tests showed that extracts from the bean gum lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples. HPV levels also fell by 80% in oral rinse samples.

The researchers then engineered the bean gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide capable of killing harmful bacteria. A single dose brought levels of Pg and Fn down to almost zero.

Importantly, the treatment did not appear to harm the beneficial bacteria that normally live in the mouth. Radiation therapy can have a different effect, reducing helpful bacteria while encouraging the growth of disease-causing yeast (Candida albicans).

A Potential Addition to Cancer Treatment

The ability to target dangerous microbes while preserving the healthy oral microbiome could make the gum useful in several ways. Researchers believe it may eventually serve as an additional therapy alongside current cancer treatments or as a preventive measure against infection and transmission.

"Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

Other authors include Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.

The research received support from NIH (grant 5-R01-HL 107904-13 awarded to Henry Daniell), the Academic Senate Grant of the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (the Surgical Education Research program), and the National Cancer Institute Cancer Center (Support Grant P30 CA168524).

articles.title: Engineered yeast that make cancer drugs could spare a rare flower
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02428-1Modified baker’s yeast can produce a precursor for a drug that is usually derived from an endangered plant and its relatives.
articles.content:
RESEARCH HIGHLIGHT

04 August 2026 Engineered yeast that make cancer drugs could spare a rare flower Modified baker’s yeast can produce a precursor for a drug that is usually derived from an endangered plant and its relatives.

The endangered plant Sinopodophyllum hexandrum is among the sources of a precursor for two cancer therapies. Credit: Felis Images/Nature Picture Library

Every year, millions of people take the drugs etoposide and teniposide, which are used to treat cancers of the lung, blood and other organs. But the process of manufacturing both drugs is low-yield and complicated. It also relies on precursors from plants in the subfamily Podophylloideae, including the endangered plant Sinopodophyllum hexandrum (also known as Podophyllum hexandrum), which is native to high-altitude Himalayan regions. Now, researchers have detailed a new pathway for making the drugs — with help from baker’s yeast1.

articles.title: Why the need for the WHO has never been greater
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 04 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02358-yDiseases don’t stop at borders. Pandemics, climate change and conflicts demand a collective approach.
articles.content:
This July marked 80 years since representatives of 61 states signed the constitution of the World Health Organization (WHO) in New York City. The founders understood that diseases do not respect borders, and that progress depends on countries working towards a common goal.

Africa’s response to this Ebola outbreak shows how to shape global health

Over the past eight decades, working with more than 190 member states and other partners, the WHO has helped to eradicate smallpox, driven progress towards wiping out polio, expanded access to life-saving vaccines and led the global fight against HIV. It has strengthened health-care systems, set health standards and helped to save millions of lives through efforts to improve tobacco control, water and air quality and sanitation.

As a result, people today live more than 25 years longer, on average, than they did 80 years ago. Far fewer women die during pregnancy and childbirth, and many more children survive and thrive past their fifth birthday.

These health gains come down to one choice: cooperation over isolation. Events this year show that the vision behind the WHO constitution is just as necessary today.

When physicians and AI work together, who is accountable? How to lay out medical liability

The current Ebola epidemic in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, cases of measles surging across the Americas and the now-ended hantavirus outbreak are reminders that health threats can emerge anywhere and affect anyone. The COVID-19 pandemic, the most severe health crisis in a century, showed that no country can tackle such health threats alone.

The WHO’s strength lies in its ability to bring together health leaders, scientists and the global health community to tackle shared challenges and find solutions, to set global standards and coordinate action in times of crisis. That value was demonstrated again last year, when member states adopted the WHO Pandemic Agreement. This treaty applies the lessons of COVID-19 to make the world more equitable and better prepared for future pandemics.

But cooperation isn’t enough: countries also need greater capacity to respond to health crises. The WHO’s Universal Health and Preparedness Review helps countries to identify gaps in their ability to respond to health emergencies. Through the Pandemic Fund, the WHO and the World Bank have supported projects in 70 countries to strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory networks, health workforces and coordination across sectors.

It emphasizes the importance of collective action against pandemics and health crises, showcasing ongoing efforts like the WHO Pandemic Agreement and capacity-building initiatives that benefit global populations.

articles.title: 3D-printed bone implants that release drugs as they heal
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Czech researchers at the University of Chemistry and Technology in Prague are building titanium joint implants with a porous internal structure designed to hold medication and release it gradually after surgery. The project is a collaboration with surgeons at Motol University Hospital. The implants use laser powder bed fusion: […]
The post 3D-printed bone implants that release drugs as they heal first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Czech researchers at the University of Chemistry and Technology in Prague are building titanium joint implants with a porous internal structure designed to hold medication and release it gradually after surgery. The project is a collaboration with surgeons at Motol University Hospital.

The implants use laser powder bed fusion: a thin layer of titanium powder is spread, a laser fuses it into shape, and the process repeats roughly 1,300 times for a knee implant. The full print takes about ten and a half hours. Researcher Jiří Kubásek calls the machine “extremely precise,” capable of recreating the microscopic architecture of actual bone.

Why the porous structure matters

“Bone tissue isn’t solid. It’s naturally porous, which allows body fluids to circulate through it,” Kubásek said. “The pores are only tens to hundreds of micrometers wide, and this printer allows us to recreate structures of exactly that scale.”

Porous implants bond better with surrounding bone because tissue can grow into the gaps. But the pores also work as drug reservoirs. One version in testing uses a carrier of sulfates, phosphates, and silver, with the antibiotic vancomycin mixed in, to ward off post-operative infection.

The hard part

Professor Dalibor Vojtěch, who leads part of the project, says the main technical problem is finding a carrier material that is safe for the body and breaks down at a controlled rate. The medication has to release gradually, not in one dose. The team hasn’t solved that yet, but they’ve already demonstrated implants for the hip, shoulder, and ankle.

Post-operative infection is one of the worst complications of joint replacement. Loading preventive medication directly into the implant, rather than relying on systemic antibiotics, is what the whole project is really about.

**Contexto** – Las infecciones después de una cirugía de reemplazo articular pueden dificultar la recuperación. Los investigadores buscan nuevas formas de evitar estas infecciones justo donde se coloca el implante.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos de la Universidad de Química y Tecnología en Praga, en colaboración con cirujanos del Hospital Universitario Motol, crearon implantes óseos de titanio usando impresión 3D. Estos implantes tienen pequeños agujeros, como el hueso real, que pueden contener medicamentos. Los medicamentos se liberan poco a poco después de la cirugía para combatir infecciones. El implante se fabrica con un láser que funde polvo de titanio capa por capa, tomando unas diez horas y media para un implante de rodilla.

**Impacto** – El diseño poroso permite que el hueso del paciente crezca dentro del implante, mejorando su ajuste y la curación. Al mismo tiempo, los poros funcionan como pequeños depósitos de medicamentos, liberando antibióticos justo donde se necesitan. Esto podría reducir las infecciones tras la cirugía, un problema serio para los pacientes.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores aún trabajan para encontrar el mejor material que contenga y libere el medicamento de forma segura y constante. Ya han fabricado implantes para cadera, hombro y tobillo y seguirán probando para asegurar que la liberación de medicamentos sea efectiva y segura.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Nuevos implantes óseos impresos en 3D con poros diminutos pueden liberar medicamentos lentamente para evitar infecciones y ayudar a una mejor recuperación tras cirugías articulares.
